newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr up in Tokyo, rise limited despite U.S. attack.
newsitem.headline: Dlr up in Tokyo, rise limited despite U.S. attack.

text.p: 0705 GMT 2400 GMT LATE EUROPE
By George Nishiyama

The dollar was standing higher in late Tokyo trade on Tuesday, but was off earlier highs as heavy sales mainly from Japanese exporters crushed a brief rally triggered by the U.S. missile attack on Iraq, dealers said.
Higher on the list of concerns was the U.S. rate outlook ahead of a slew of economic data due this week, they added.
"What's important are the (U.S.) indicators and what they mean for U.S. credit policy," said Ichiro Ikeda, vice president at Goldman Sachs International Bank in Tokyo.
Although the dollar rose as high as 109.35 yen and near 1.49 marks after the U.S. action, it met sales by exporters at around 109.30 yen and soon retreated, dealers said.
"There was a huge offer at 109.30 yen. And from the way it was just sitting there throughout the rally suggests that it must have been from exporters," said a trust bank dealer.
Sales from non-life insurers were also detected above 109.30 yen, dealers said.
Dealers also played down the significance of the U.S. attack, pointing out that it was unlikely to lead to a prolonged confrontation such as the Gulf War.

"It's a one-time event and will be limited as long as the issue is the Kurds," said Yasuhito Kawashima, chief manager at Toyo Trust & Banking Co, adding the dollar's rise will be limited to 109.50 yen and 1.4950 marks.

Although some dealers said the consequent rise in oil prices may lead to inflation fears in the United States and hurt the dollar, others said damage to the Japanese economy would offset the negative impact on the dollar.
"In general, a rise in oil prices would hurt the Japanese economy and lead to yen sales," said Goldman's Ikeda.
"But there is a chance that it could set off inflation fears in the U.S.," said Takuma Kurosawa, chief manager with Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp.

Dealers said views that the Federal Reserve may opt to raise rates at its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on September 24 were gaining support amid the recent release of strong U.S. economic data.
But a pre-emptive credit tightening is largely seen giving support to the dollar, dealers said.
A U.S. tightening would widen the interest rate gap between the United States and Japan and further undermine the yen, Toyo Trust's Kawashima said.
Earlier in the afternoon, the dollar was given a brief lift on a media report that the Fed was mulling a bigger-than-expected rate hike.

The Wall Street Journal reported in its Tuesday edition that the policy makers were leaning towards raising the federal funds target rate half a percentage point, if key economic data showed an overheating economy. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk (81-3-5473-3710)
